question_bank.stem: A new neural network is close to working, but training is unstable and slow. Which first tuning lever most closely matches the lecture's explicit example of a high-value hyperparameter?

options.text: The batch size.
The learning rate.
The label smoothing target.
The train-dev split.

question_bank.rationale: Ng explicitly names the learning rate as an example of a high-leverage hyperparameter to tune.

question_bank.stem: In a multi-stage face-recognition door system, what habit did the lecture present as the biggest separator between teams that ship in weeks and teams that wander for months?

options.text: Replacing the pipeline with one giant end-to-end model immediately.
Adding more security rules before measuring where errors enter the pipeline.
Running a disciplined diagnostic process to decide which part to fix next.
Collecting every available video stream before checking current failure modes.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture emphasizes disciplined diagnostics in complex ML systems, not random work or premature large changes.

source_ref.evidence_span: than many months, is the ability to drive a disciplined

frame_evidence.visual_description: Board shows C3 Strategy for ML projects while he explains how systematic diagnostics speed up project execution.

question_bank.stem: Your team read a paper saying more data helps, and someone proposes a six-month data-collection effort immediately. According to the lecture, what is the better diagnostic stance?

options.text: Approve the collection plan, because additional data is almost always the safest first move.
Approve the plan only after buying more GPUs, because data and compute should scale together.
Delay all modeling work until the larger dataset arrives, because interim results are misleading.
Check whether more data is actually the bottleneck before committing months to collection.

question_bank.rationale: Ng warns against blindly collecting more data just because a paper or trend says to; diagnostics should identify the real bottleneck first.

source_ref.evidence_span: So let's go spend six months to collect more data.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Instructor stands beside the C3 ML-project-strategy notes while warning against hype-driven data collection.

question_bank.stem: A manager wants to solve weak results by purchasing a large GPU budget right away. What response best matches the lecture?

options.text: First diagnose whether compute is the limiting factor before spending heavily on GPUs.
Buy the GPUs first, because spare compute almost always reveals the real bottleneck.
Skip diagnosis and switch to a larger model, because compute shortages and model shortages are equivalent.
Avoid using GPUs at all, because project strategy matters more when models train on CPUs.

question_bank.rationale: The lecture treats GPU purchases as a decision that should follow diagnosis, not as a reflexive cure-all.

source_ref.evidence_span: Maybe you should buy more GPUs.

frame_evidence.visual_description: Same ML-project-strategy whiteboard remains visible as he discusses whether GPUs are truly the bottleneck.

question_bank.stem: On a greenfield problem with no close precedents, how did the lecture recommend estimating how much data you may ultimately need?

options.text: Start by writing a formula for sample complexity before collecting any examples.
Gather some data, train an initial model, and use its behavior to calibrate the next data decision.
Wait until you can collect the full dataset, because early pilots understate eventual performance.
Choose the data target from a benchmark in another domain, because transfer estimates are usually reliable enough.

question_bank.rationale: For greenfield tasks, the lecture recommends an empirical pilot: train an initial model and let its results inform the next data decision.

source_ref.evidence_span: And the degree to which your initial model works or does not

frame_evidence.visual_description: Instructor closes the greenfield-data answer while still in front of the whiteboard, emphasizing an empirical first-model check.
